dies.asset: The render layer — ~4,700 lines of app.js (57 panel renderers + 5 screens + 6 wizard steps; `openEquipment` 579 lines, `renderTimelinePanel` 517, `openCut` 159, `openKeyManager` 155, `cPaintProjects` 132)
dies.whyLost: Template-literal `innerHTML` plus manual `addEventListener` wiring has no mechanical path to JSX. Every one of these is a hand-rolled render + hand-rolled event binding + hand-rolled re-render; a component model replaces all three at once. Measured: 1,228 lines contain raw HTML tags, 819 lines are direct DOM manipulation. This is the honest ~40% loss and no condition saves the *shape* of it.
dies.couldWeSaveIt: Not the code — but three things inside it can be rescued and must be, BEFORE any port: (1) the plan pipeline buried in `buildList()` (see the conditional entry below), (2) the id/class/data-attr contract, so the tests that target it survive, (3) the copy. Every user-facing string is already a static `L(he,en)` literal that ports verbatim into JSX. Realistically ~60% of a panel's *value* (logic + strings + CSS) survives and ~40% (the markup/wiring) is retyped.

dies.asset: Navigation: `panelStack` (93 call sites of showPanel/openFrom/panelBack), `cNavGo`/`CSCREENS`, `cWiz.step` — 74 navigable surfaces
dies.whyLost: There is nothing to preserve. Verified by grep: `pushState`/`replaceState`/`popstate`/`hashchange`/`location.hash` occurrences in app.js = **0**. Navigation is three non-communicating layers of CSS class toggles held in plain JS variables, and `panelStack` holds *closures* — non-serializable by construction, so no view has an identity a URL or a history entry could name. `closePanel()` (bound to ✕, Escape AND backdrop) does `panelStack=[]`, destroying the whole stack.
dies.couldWeSaveIt: Nothing to save, but a lot to *place*. The replacement — a serializable panel-descriptor registry + History API — is already designed in `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-24-navigation-model-design.md` (draft, awaiting owner approval; §2.1 inventories all 74 surfaces). Build that registry in **vanilla now**. It is the exact data structure React Router consumes. Build it now and a future router migration is a mapping exercise; skip it and React 'gives you routing' only by rewriting all 74 surfaces from scratch.

dies.asset: `build.py` as an inliner (699 lines): the `__CSS__`/`__JS__`/`__DATA__`/`__I18N_DICTS__` substitution, the single-file `dist/index.html`, and the generated service worker
dies.whyLost: A bundler (Vite/esbuild) owns this job in a React world. The single-file property is not automatic — it must be re-chosen deliberately via `vite-plugin-singlefile`, and if it is not, the PWA offline shell, the TWA path, and the test harness (below) all change underneath you at the same moment.
dies.couldWeSaveIt: The *inlining* dies; the **assertions must not go with it**. See the conditional entry on Guards A/B/C/D — extract them into a standalone checker now and this becomes a pure loss of ~150 lines of plumbing instead of a silent loss of the whole i18n safety net.

dies.asset: The four ad-hoc tool launchers (☰ More sheet 27 slots, home dock 11, AI hub 5, `openTools` 15 — 58 launch slots, 3 live, 0 producing a working back button)
dies.whyLost: They are dispatch tables of `window[fnName]()` string lookups. Under a bundler, `window[fn]` resolution stops working entirely (the functions are no longer globals), and the dispatch pattern itself is the source of the two-level back-button loss the nav audit found.
dies.couldWeSaveIt: The *slot inventory* (which tool appears where, the user's customized dock order in `mk-homecustom`) is data and survives. The dispatch mechanism should be replaced by the panel registry (same work as the navigation entry) — do it once, in vanilla, and the launchers become table-driven rather than string-eval-driven.

dies.whyLost: These exist *only* because the plan pipeline is a closure inside a render function and sibling scopes cannot reach its results. They are a symptom, not an asset. In a module world they become return values.
dies.couldWeSaveIt: Deliberately do not save them. But note that `window._wpTasks` is read by voice-cook mode and `window._wpCtx` by `wireRows()` — both are live consumers, so the ORCH extraction must give them a real interface, not just delete the stashes.

**C · THE REACT MIGRATION ITSELF**
- *If done AFTER A:* build pipeline (Vite + singlefile plugin + DATA/dict injection + SW) 1 CP2 · shell + routing driven by the existing registry + theme/appearance 1 CP2 · 57 panels + 5 screens + 6 wizard steps ported markup-preserving 3.5–5 CP2 (`openEquipment` and `renderTimelinePanel` are ~1 CP2 each on their own) · re-anchoring the 263 mixed tests + fixture rework 0.5–1 CP2. **≈ 6–8 CP2 (66–88 tasks).**

**The number that answers the owner's question:** the preservation work (4 CP2) is work already on his roadmap, and it cuts the migration from ~15 CP2 to ~7 CP2. Net: he pays 4 to save 8, and the 4 ship user-visible value (navigation, closed gaps) on their own. The 15-CP2 version — migrating cold — *is* the "כתיבה מחדש" he is afraid of, and his fear is correctly calibrated.

**Not counted anywhere above because it is free:** the Python data layer (115 KB of `data.py`, 279 cited cut-source entries, 1,008 URLs in `sources.py`), the 7 shipped language dictionaries (1,536 chrome keys + ~700 KB of data dict per language), the Cloudflare Worker (91 lines), 1,780 lines of CSS, and every specification and audit document. These cross the boundary at zero cost.
headline: Your fear is correctly aimed but at the wrong target: the thing that would be thrown away is not "the app" — it is one specific ~500-line region, the plan pipeline sitting as a private closure inside `renderTimelinePanel.buildList()`, plus 501 of 800 Playwright tests that reach the app through bare global identifiers a bundler deletes. Everything you would most hate to lose is already portable: I verified that `itemStages`, `itemPaths`, `effectiveSchedule`, `planSchedule`, `schedulePlacements`, `cookerContention`, `methodRules` and `equipPlan` contain **zero** DOM references and **zero** store reads, and `equipment.js`/EQM is already a clean module with a build guard. The Python data layer, the 279 citations, the 7 shipped language dictionaries and the Worker cross the boundary at literally zero cost. But React buys you **none of your three named drivers** — navigation is the History API plus a serializable panel registry (design already drafted; `pushState` occurrences in app.js today = 0), and realtime plus cross-device sync are a Cloudflare Worker and D1, framework-agnostic on both counts. Do the four preservation moves inside the current codebase, ship your three drivers in vanilla, and let React become a maintainability decision you make later at half the price.
openQuestions: **What does "realtime currency" actually mean?** (a) my phone and my PC show my own edits within seconds — that is last-write-wins blob sync plus poll-on-focus on the Worker you already run, ~1.5 CP2, no framework implication. (b) several people at one cookout share a live plan — that is presence, conflict semantics and a different product. The answer changes the estimate by 3x and it is the single biggest unknown in this analysis.

**Is the PC a viewer or a full editor?** A big-screen workplan viewer is a read-only render of the same JSON — cheap, no framework change, and arguably the highest-value/lowest-cost feature on this whole list. A full second editor multiplies the sync design.

**Will you approve the navigation redesign shipping in vanilla first?** `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-24-navigation-model-design.md` is drafted and awaiting your approval, and it carries a flagged §4 Waiver-Gate notice (a reinterpretation of D5 and a consequence of D6) that must be raised in conversation, not inherited from a document. Your answer decides whether "navigation" remains a React driver at all.

**Must the single-file PWA property survive a bundler?** It is currently load-bearing in three places at once: the offline service-worker shell, the Google Play TWA path, and the test harness's `route.fulfill` in-memory doc trick. `vite-plugin-singlefile` preserves it — but only if chosen deliberately at the start, and it constrains code-splitting forever after.

**Does the app still have to work with no network?** CLAUDE.md records the 2026-07-22 ONLINE-FIRST decision, but the sync design in `04a-architecture.md` §4 still says "localStorage stays source of truth; sync is background reconcile." Those two are not in conflict yet, but D1 landing is the moment they must be reconciled explicitly.

**Is anyone else going to write UI code?** This is the honest React question. For one author, a component framework is a preference. For two, the 500-line render functions become an onboarding and merge-conflict tax that a framework genuinely fixes.

**How much of the 2.42 MB payload is the data layer, and does a server change that?** Once D1 exists, the premium catalog *could* move behind the proxy (04a §5 calls that the only real IP protection). That is a bigger architectural fork than React and it is currently unscheduled.
recommendation:
**Do not migrate now. Make the migration cheap instead — and ship your three drivers without React.**

Four moves, in this order. All four are work you want anyway; all four are already on your registered roadmap or in a drafted spec.

**1 · Extract ORCH before anything else (1.5 CP2).** Lift the plan pipeline out of `renderTimelinePanel.buildList()` into `orchestrator.js`, in the exact `equipment.js`/EQM shape. This is the one asset that genuinely dies in a migration and the one whose loss would be unrecoverable, because it carries the safety invariants. Your own BIG-STATUS names it: S2, 25 gaps, "a private closure inside a render fn; only 5 window exports" — I verified 15 `window._X=` stashes total, which is what a function that cannot return does. Extracting it closes the largest common-cause cluster in the programme (13 gaps) *and* removes the migration's biggest risk. Same work, two payoffs.

**2 · Adopt one `MK` namespace and ban new bare-global test access (0.75 CP2).** 501 of 800 tests reach the app as `deviceCapacity(equipByCat('smoker')[0])` — bare identifiers in string-evaluated code. Under any bundler those identifiers do not exist. Expose the logic layer as one object, codemod the evaluate sites, and a future bundle needs one line (`if (DEV||TEST) window.MK = {…}`) for all 501 to pass unchanged. Starting today, every new v5-harvest function goes on `MK` and every new test targets `MK.fn` — zero cost now, and it makes the ~150 code blocks you are about to write the first 150 that are already migration-ready.

**3 · Get the i18n guards out of `build.py` and teach the extractor about multiple files (0.5 CP2).** `scripts/i18n-extract.mjs` reads exactly one file (`args[0] || 'app.js'`), and Guard D hashes only `_js`. This is not a future problem — it bites on your *next* module extraction. `rules.js` is that extraction. The moment a `L('…','…')` literal lives outside app.js it is silently dropped from `_extracted.json`, Guard A never sees it, and it ships untranslated to 7 languages. (`equipment.js` has 0 `L()` calls, which is the only reason nobody has hit this yet.) Fix: extractor takes a file list; Guards A/B/C/D move into a standalone checker invocable from CI; add the acorn-jsx plugin while you are in there so the extractor is JSX-ready for free. Also, at this second extraction, do what the roadmap already tells you to do — generalize `build.py`'s hardcoded `equipment.js` block into a MODULES list with per-module F5 guards.

**4 · Ship navigation in vanilla, from the spec you already have (1.25 CP2).** History API + a serializable panel-descriptor registry replacing `panelStack`'s closures. This delivers hardware Back, deep links, and shareable workplan URLs — the actual user value you attributed to React — and the registry it produces is precisely what React Router would consume later. Approve or amend `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-24-navigation-model-design.md` (note it carries a flagged Waiver-Gate item that must be raised in conversation).

**Then, separately and framework-agnostically, build the server (2.5 CP2):** extend the Worker you already run with `/sync` + D1 + last-write-wins on `updatedAt`, per `04a-architecture.md` §2b/§4. Cross-device sync and realtime currency have nothing to do with React. Do not let the two decisions travel together — that bundling is exactly how a reasonable architecture change turns into a rewrite.

**Revisit React when a trigger below fires**, not on a date. If it fires after these four moves, the port is ~7 CP2 with the engine, the tests, the guards, the routing model and the styling all intact. If you do it cold today it is ~15 CP2 with the safety net down — and that version *is* the rewrite you are afraid of.

**One thing to change in the work you are about to build, above all others:** make the v5 harvest emit **data, not prose**. `itemStages` today returns `` label: `${smokeLbl} ${coldT}°` `` — a localized string with the number baked in. The rules.js design already says "typed codes only, never prose"; extend that rule to the Wave-0 wrap stage, to the outcome vectors, and to CP2's rows: `{kind:'wrap', code:'WRAP_AT_CORE', params:{coreC:75}, cite:{…}}`, with a render-side `stageLabel(stage)` doing the `L()`. That single discipline makes the engine framework-immune, and it independently fixes L13 (a number that is a param can be wrapped in a `dir="ltr"` island; a number baked into a string cannot).

risks.risk: Rewriting the plan pipeline from scratch re-derives safety behaviour *while the safety net is down*. The 501 pure-evaluate tests all break at the same instant a bundler lands (bare-global access), and `safety-invariant.spec.ts`, `p0-safety-nums.spec.ts` (18 tests) and `p0-spoken-safety.spec.ts` (32 tests, 31 of them pure-evaluate) are in that set. You would be re-implementing the code that computes `safe`, `bcheck` and cook durations at the exact moment the tests that guard them cannot run.
risks.mitigation: Hard sequencing rule: extract ORCH and adopt the `MK` namespace as two separate, individually-green changes BEFORE any bundler or framework work begins. Never let a framework change and a logic move land in the same phase. If a migration ever starts, the entry gate is `npx playwright test` green with the `MK` access path already in place.

risks.risk: The i18n Guards are welded into `build.py`. Swapping the build tool silently removes Guard A (which today *aborts the build* when a known key lacks a translation in an active language), Guard B (numeric/unit drift across 7 languages), Guard C (translator prompt-echo garbage) and Guard D. Nothing fails loudly — you just start shipping English leaks and drifted numbers to 6 languages again, which is a failure mode this project has already paid for twice (v267, v269/v270).
risks.mitigation: Extract the guards into a standalone checker (`verify_i18n.py` or a node script) wired into CI *now*, before any bundler discussion. The guards then survive any build-tool change by construction. Cost ~0.5 CP2, and it is needed for the next module extraction regardless.

risks.risk: Someone 'modernizes' the i18n key convention during the port. The 7 shipped dictionaries are keyed by the **Hebrew source string** (1,536 chrome keys plus `__names__`, plus ~700 KB of data dict per language). Moving to synthetic keys (`t('card.brisket.title')`) invalidates every language at once — the single largest destroy-in-one-commit risk in the repo.
risks.mitigation: Write the key convention down as a binding contract before any migration plan is drafted: *keys are the Hebrew source string; `L(he,en)` is a plain function call and is legal inside JSX expression containers unchanged.* No renaming, no namespacing, no i18next migration. The dictionaries are framework-immune precisely because of this property.

risks.risk: The warm-page test fixture's `route.fulfill` optimisation assumes a single-file `dist/index.html`. Under a multi-file bundle, each of ~800 `seedApp` reloads also refetches the JS chunk over loopback — and `serve.js` sets no cache headers (verified). This reintroduces the exact Windows loopback-serialization stall the project spent a whole arc curing (measured 286 s → 12 s on the reload-storm harness; suite 3.0 m → ~54 s). It would present as unexplained flake, and the root cause is already documented as easy to misdiagnose.
risks.mitigation: Decide up front: either `vite-plugin-singlefile` so the fixture keeps working byte-for-byte, or extend the fulfill route to the chunk paths. Either way, re-measure with the reload-storm harness (`docs/research/flake-refactor-rootcause.md`) before accepting the new build — do not assume.

risks.risk: A CSS methodology change (CSS Modules, Tailwind, styled-components) rides along with the framework change. That discards 1,780 lines including all the RTL/bidi tuning, the `dir="ltr"` numeric islands, the theme tokens and the occupancy-view visual grammar — plus the 104 class selectors the tests use.
risks.mitigation: Global CSS stays global. React does not require a styling change and coupling the two is how a 7-CP2 port becomes a 12-CP2 one. Make this an explicit non-goal in whatever plan authorises a migration.

risks.risk: A markup 'cleanup' during the port. The 263 mixed + 36 pure-DOM tests target 137 distinct `#id`s, 104 classes and 73 `data-*` attributes. Preserved markup ⇒ they mostly survive; restructured markup ⇒ they all need re-anchoring, and re-anchoring a test is where assertions quietly get weakened.
risks.mitigation: Freeze the current id/class/data-attr set as a written contract at the start of any port, and port markup-preserving. Separately: the repo has **0** `data-testid` today — start adding a stable hook to each new CP2/rules surface now, so the newest tests are the most portable ones.

risks.risk: Losing the single-file PWA property by accident. It is load-bearing in three unrelated places simultaneously — the offline service-worker shell, the Google Play TWA path (`04a-architecture.md` §1), and the test harness — so it can be lost once and hurt three times.
risks.mitigation: Treat 'the shipped artifact is one file' as an explicit requirement in any build-tool decision, and verify it with the existing `foot-news.spec.ts` / delivery-shell tests plus a live `.foot-stamp` probe per §10.10.

risks.risk: Scope creep from bundling the three decisions (React, client/server, database) into one move. They are independent: the Worker and D1 need no framework change, and the framework change needs no server.
risks.mitigation: Three separate phase plans, three separate owner approvals. Any plan that proposes two of them together should be treated as a Waiver-Gate event and raised in conversation.

risks.risk: `itemStages` bakes localized prose and interpolated numbers into `label`/`note` (19 `L()` calls inside the function). Any framework that re-renders on language change must re-run the *engine* to change the text, which couples presentation to the safety-bearing computation and blocks `dir="ltr"` islands on those figures.
risks.mitigation: This is the highest-value single fix and it belongs in the v5 harvest, not in a migration: stage objects carry `{kind, code, params:{tempC, hours}, cite}` and a render-side `stageLabel(stage)` does the `L()` lookup. Apply it first to the Wave-0 wrap stage, which is new code anyway, then retrofit by attrition.

survives.survivesHow: SURVIVES ~100%. I measured every one of these function bodies: **zero** `document`/`innerHTML`/`querySelector`/`addEventListener`/`classList` references and **zero** `store.get`/`store.set` calls. They are already pure JS over plain objects. A React port copies these files across unchanged; a bundler only changes how they are loaded. This is the most important fact in the whole analysis — the part you would least want to re-derive is the part that is already framework-agnostic.
survives.condition: ONE condition, and it applies to the work you are about to build: `itemStages` currently returns stage objects whose `label`/`note` are **already-rendered localized strings with numbers interpolated** (19 `L()` calls inside it; e.g. ``label: `${smokeLbl} ${coldT}°` ``). Change the convention now — stage objects carry `{kind, code, params:{tempC, hours}, cite}` and a render-side `stageLabel(stage)` does the localization. Apply it to the Wave-0 wrap stage (new code, free) and retrofit the rest by attrition.

Under a bundler it becomes an ES module with named exports; the F5 guard becomes an import-graph assertion. survives.survivesHow: CONDITIONAL, and this one has a live bug you will hit before any migration. Guards B and C are pure text checks over the dictionaries and survive anything. And `i18n-extract.mjs` reads exactly ONE file: `const inputPath = args[0] || 'app.js'`. **The next module you extract from app.js silently drops its `L()` keys from `_extracted.json`.** `equipment.js` has 0 `L()` calls, which is the only reason this has not fired yet — and `rules.js` is the next extraction.
survives.condition: Three cheap changes NOW: (1) the extractor takes a **file list**, not one path; (2) Guard D's signature covers that same list; (3) all four guards move out of `build.py` into a standalone checker invoked from CI, so a future bundler swap cannot take them with it. While you are there, add the `acorn-jsx` plugin — acorn cannot parse JSX, and that one line is the difference between the extractor surviving a React port and being rewritten.

Under any bundler those identifiers do not exist in global scope and all 501 fail at the *access path*. But the assertions, the fixtures, the seeded state and the domain knowledge inside them are untouched — this is a mechanical break, not a semantic one.

triggers: **A second person starts writing UI code.** Today the 500-line render functions (`openEquipment` 579, `renderTimelinePanel` 517) are one author's working memory. With two authors they become a merge-conflict and onboarding tax that a component model genuinely fixes. This is the honest React trigger and nothing else on this list is.

**A single render function crosses ~800 lines, or the render layer crosses ~6,000 lines.** Currently 579 max and ~4,700 total. That is the measurable point where hand-rolled re-render bugs start costing more than a framework would.

**A panel must be reachable by URL** — sharing a workplan, a push notification deep-linking to a live cook, a marketing landing page. That is the navigation trigger, and it should be answered with the History API + panel registry, NOT with React.
**The first paying subscriber exists.** Cross-device sync stops being a feature and becomes a promise. Build Worker `/sync` + D1 then — no framework implication.

**Two surfaces must show the same live state at once** (copilot on the phone while the workplan is on a PC). That is the realtime trigger. Answer with a Worker + SSE or a Durable Object; still framework-neutral.

**You find yourself writing manual DOM-diffing code** — reconciling a list in place rather than re-rendering it — to keep a view from flickering or losing scroll position. That is the framework asking to be hired, and it is a much more reliable signal than any roadmap date.

**An iOS App Store listing with native IAP becomes revenue-relevant.** The answer there is Capacitor, not React (Apple Guideline 4.2 rejects raw PWA wrappers, per `04a-architecture.md` §1) — but if that path ever forces a component framework, the four preservation moves are what make it affordable rather than a rewrite.

**A NON-trigger, stated explicitly so it does not creep in:** language count. The dictionaries are keyed by Hebrew source strings and survive any framework; going from 7 to 23 languages is not a reason to touch React.
